axes.question: Do organisations explicitly use litigation to seek legal or policy change?
What resources finance strategic-litigation capacity and is case-specific tasking documented?
Do courts independently filter NGO strategic claims rather than mechanically implement them?
Can successful strategic litigation create binding legal or institutional change?

axes.gap: Implementation is documented as a separate stage but complete compliance is not established across cases.
axes.question: Are judgments fully implemented and how is execution monitored?

axes.gap: No comparative causal design establishes system-wide durable counterfactual political effect.
axes.question: What durable political effect is attributable counterfactually to strategic litigation?

causal.counter: Court independence, adverse judgments, implementation failures, independent policy drivers and absence of case-level donor tasking interrupt or confound downstream edges.
causal.gap: External donor tasking and durable counterfactual political effect remain unestablished.
causal.limit: I6 is supported case-specifically for legal/institutional change; implementation is heterogeneous and I7 durable counterfactual political effect is not established.

claims.claim: Strategic litigation is an intentional influence mechanism used by civil-society organisations to seek changes in law and practice through courts.
claims.gap: Intentional influence does not by itself make the practice abusive or illegitimate.

claims.claim: Organisational funding can enable litigation capacity, but the examined evidence does not establish that core or project donors directed specific cases, arguments or requested judgments.
claims.gap: Case-level earmarking/tasking records are absent in examined material.

claims.claim: Courts function as independent filters rather than passive instruments of NGO strategy; strategic cases can win, lose or be redirected procedurally.
claims.gap: Judicial independence in a given system does not exclude every form of pressure; no such pressure is established here.

claims.claim: Successful strategic litigation can create binding legal obligations or doctrinal change with material institutional consequences.
claims.gap: Binding judgment does not establish full implementation or durable political effect.

claims.claim: Judgment, implementation and durable political effect are separate causal stages; post-judgment monitoring and execution procedures are often necessary.
claims.gap: Counterfactual long-run policy effect remains case-specific.

claims.claim: The evidence supports lawful strategic litigation as a real channel of political/legal influence but does not support a general classification of NGO rights litigation as covert interference, capture or abusive lawfare.
claims.gap: Abusive procedure or external tasking must be proven case by case.

controls.control: Funding control: core/project/public funding establishes capacity or permitted purpose, not donor command of a specific lawsuit.
Outcome control: BLOOM and GISTI/LDH/Cimade losses show strategic intent and access to court do not guarantee judicial success.
Implementation control: Affaire du Siècle and KlimaSeniorinnen require post-judgment execution/follow-up; a win is not identical to implemented policy.
Democratic-boundary control: ECtHR itself states climate adjudication is complementary to democratic decision-making.

Qualification control: strategic litigation is deliberate influence through law but is lawful advocacy by default unless abuse, deception, unlawful coercion or hidden tasking is separately established.
Association control: common values, donor overlap or coalition intervention do not establish a single command structure.

facts.subject: ECRE strategic litigation objective
facts.value: ECRE states that its strategic litigation aims to support asylum seekers and refugees through courts and to effect deeper legal changes through litigation.

facts.subject: ECRE strategic litigation methods
facts.value: ECRE defines strategic litigation broadly to include direct case engagement, third-party interventions, support to lawyers, training, evidence statements and monitoring implementation of judgments.

facts.subject: ECRE expenditure and work areas
facts.value: ECRE reported EUR 1.6 million annual expenditure for 2024 and listed Legal Support/Litigation, Advocacy and Communications as its three work areas.

facts.subject: ECRE funding mix
facts.value: ECRE reported that 43% of 2024 income came from core grants; other income included project funding, membership fees and small amounts from events/expertise, and it named JRCT, EPIM and OSF among long-term donors reducing or withdrawing funding.

facts.subject: ECRE litigation outputs
facts.value: ECRE reported six direct interventions before UN treaty bodies or the ECtHR, emergency litigation support for three high-impact cases and legal advice on more than 40 queries in 2024.

facts.subject: ECRE evaluation of litigation support
facts.value: ECRE reported an independent evaluation commissioned at a donor request which concluded that its legal-support/litigation work improved litigation quality and outcomes; the claim is retained as an evaluation reported by ECRE, not as independently reproduced causal evidence in this run.

facts.subject: OSF strategic litigation method
facts.value: Open Society Foundations describes grantmaking, research, advocacy, impact investment and strategic litigation as methods it uses to pursue rights and dignity.

facts.subject: Affaire du Siècle judicial injunction
facts.value: The Conseil d’Etat 2024 decision recounts that the Paris administrative court ordered the Prime Minister and relevant ministers in October 2021 to take useful measures to repair ecological harm corresponding to an uncompensated 15 Mt CO2eq gap from the first carbon budget.

facts.subject: Affaire du Siècle implementation dispute
facts.value: Oxfam France, Greenpeace France and Notre Affaire à Tous pursued execution of the 2021 judgment; the Conseil d’Etat held in December 2024 that the challenge was an appeal within the jurisdiction of the Paris administrative court of appeal rather than deciding the implementation merits itself.

facts.subject: Grande-Synthe NGO interventions
facts.value: In the Grande-Synthe climate proceedings the Conseil d’Etat admitted interventions by Oxfam France, Greenpeace France, Notre Affaire à Tous and the Fondation pour la Nature et l’Homme.

facts.subject: Grande-Synthe binding order
facts.value: The Conseil d’Etat annulled the State refusal to take additional emissions-reduction measures and ordered the Prime Minister to take all useful measures compatible with the 2030 reduction objectives before 31 March 2022.

facts.subject: BLOOM negative control
facts.value: The Conseil d’Etat rejected BLOOM’s request to annul the 2022 decree defining strong protection, showing that NGO strategic litigation does not imply control over judicial outcomes.

facts.subject: GISTI LDH Cimade negative control
facts.value: The Conseil d’Etat rejected challenges brought by GISTI, the Syndicat des avocats de France, ADDE, Cimade and the Ligue des droits de l’Homme against an immigration-related decree, providing a second negative control on outcome independence.

facts.subject: Public subsidy earmarking safeguard
facts.value: The Conseil d’Etat held that a local-authority subsidy to an association active in sea rescue required appropriate commitments ensuring the support was exclusively devoted to cooperation, development or humanitarian actions and excluded the association’s other activities.

facts.subject: Subsidy does not imply funding all NGO activities
facts.value: The subsidy ruling provides a legal counterexample to the inference that public financing of an NGO automatically finances its advocacy or litigation activities; grant purpose and safeguards must be traced.

facts.subject: NGO intervention and interim suspension
facts.value: In the Soulèvements de la Terre dissolution litigation, numerous rights, environmental and legal organisations were admitted as interveners and the Conseil d’Etat suspended execution of the dissolution decree pending the merits case.

facts.subject: KlimaSeniorinnen association standing
facts.value: The ECtHR Grand Chamber held that the applicant association had standing in the climate context while the four individual applicants did not satisfy the victim-status criteria.

facts.subject: KlimaSeniorinnen substantive violation
facts.value: The ECtHR found violations of Article 8 and Article 6 §1 and held that Switzerland had failed to comply with positive obligations concerning adequate climate-mitigation measures.

facts.subject: Judicial role remains bounded
facts.value: The ECtHR emphasized that climate measures require democratic decision-making and that domestic courts and the Court have a role complementary to those democratic processes.

facts.subject: Post-judgment implementation advocacy
facts.value: Verein KlimaSeniorinnen submitted a Rule 9.2 communication to the Committee of Ministers in February 2025 concerning execution of the ECtHR judgment, demonstrating that a judicial win and implementation follow-up are separate stages.

facts.subject: Strategic litigation is intentional influence
facts.value: ECRE’s own description and 2024 activity record establish strategic litigation as an intentional method for changing law and practice, not merely incidental participation in isolated cases.

facts.subject: Courts independently filter NGO claims
facts.value: Multiple NGO challenges were rejected on the merits or procedure, so access to court and strategic intent do not establish control of outcomes.

facts.subject: Funding-tasking boundary
facts.value: The examined funding records establish organizational resource support and, in one public-subsidy context, explicit purpose restrictions; they do not establish an external donor directing a specific case, argument or desired judgment.

facts.subject: Judgment-implementation boundary
facts.value: Strategic litigation can produce binding judicial obligations or doctrinal change, but implementation, compliance and durable policy effects require separate follow-up and cannot be inferred from the judgment alone.
